transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Vecra), Sana Iqbal (Vecra), Tom Reeves (Vecra)
Links referenced: internal benchmark spreadsheet (link), Dedicated pricing deck (sent after), sample runbook (link)

[00:00] Jordan: okay folks, thanks for joining the weekly POC sync. Um, quick rollcall — Jordan from Redwood here, Priya SE on my left.
[00:12] Priya: hey everybody.
[00:15] Carlos: hi, Carlos here. Sana and Tom also on.
[00:20] Jordan: great. Agenda is throughput results, we tuned continuous batching and concurrency targets, then queueing behavior and next steps. Priya you want to start with test summary?
[00:32] Priya: yeah sure. So we ran two sustained runs overnight, each about 30 minutes to 1 hour. One with the default batching window (we had it at 20ms) and concurrency 64, and the second with increased batch aggres — aggro? uh, aggressive windowing, 50ms, concurrency 128. Results: throughput went up ~2.3x with the 50ms / 128 concurrency setting but p99 latency increased from ~380ms to ~820ms for tail. Average token latency stayed ok ~120-150ms.
[01:06] Sana: when you say throughput went up 2.3x is that tokens per second or requests per second?
[01:12] Priya: good call — tokens/sec. Requests/sec improved ~1.7x, because some requests are longer.
[01:20] Tom: and what hardware were these on?
[01:23] Priya: Dedicated-ish test nodes: 4x A100-ish profile GPUs in our test pool (we used the Dedicated staging fleet), single model replica per GPU, quantized to int8-ish profile. There's some sloppy naming in the logs, I think the kernel labels got munged — it shows "a100_v2_sim" but it's the standard perf image.
[01:42] Carlos: okay. Our main concern is sustaining 12k tokens/sec at peak for search rerank traffic with p95 < 400ms. Right now p95 is okay on the 20ms/64 run but not at 128/50ms.
[01:57] Priya: right. So we looked at continuous batching behavior — essentially increasing the batching window increases average batch size which increases throughput but raises queueing delay for small requests. We also measured KV cache hit rates: when we warm KV caches, effective token generation improved and p95 dropped ~10-12%.
[02:20] Jordan: note — KV cache warmup might be realistic for your workload since you have repeat prefixes in the rerank path. Carlos, can you confirm how much repetition you see?
[02:31] Carlos: we see decent repetition for the same user-session but across different customers it's mixed. Maybe 20-30% reuse on prefixes. We'll share traces.
[02:40] [02:40] Priya: also observed queueing backpressure: at extreme concurrency we saw request queue growth and occasional head-of-line blocking where a long token-decoding request pushed short ones back, that raised tail latencies. We recommended a hybrid policy — strict concurrency cap for short requests + batching window tuned for mixed length.
[03:05] Tom: what is strict concurrency cap? a number?
[03:07] Priya: for your workload I'd recommend target concurrency 96 with burst up to 128 for scheduled windows. Use request-weighted concurrency where long requests count as 2 units. That's something we can implement in routing rules.
[03:20] Sana: and how does that interact with autoscaling? We need predictable cost.
[03:25] Priya: autoscaling is based on GPU utilization and queue length; if you put a hard concurrency cap, autoscaler will spin more replicas earlier to keep latency. It increases cost but stabilizes p95. Also Dedicated burst options let you have reserved baseline with on-demand burst for spikes — Jordan will share pricing.
[03:44] Jordan: yep I'll send the Dedicated pricing deck after call.
[03:48] Carlos: one more question on quantization — our internal SRE worried about quality regressions at int8 for generation. Did you run evals?
[03:56] Priya: we did a small eval using your rerank testset — int8 gave negligible score drop (<0.8% on NDCG) for this model family, but if you have stricter thresholds we can pin to int16 for critical routes. Quantization also reduces token compute so batch sizes can be larger without saturating GPU.
[04:18] Tom: good. Any notes on kernel selection or software stack? We saw logs referencing "gemm_opt_v3" and a bunch of warnings.
[04:27] Priya: yeah, that's why we want the kernel selection deep-dive — sometimes the runtime chooses a less optimal kernel for mid-length sequences. We'll look at sequence length distribution in traces and force a kernel or recompile path. That can buy you ~15% throughput.
[04:41] [05:00] Jordan: okay let's go through the concrete numbers from the spreadsheet — Priya can you read the key rows?
[05:06] Priya: sure. Baseline (20ms, c64) tokens/sec = 7.8k TPS, avg token latency 140ms, p95 token latency 360ms. Aggressive (50ms, c128) tokens/sec = 18k TPS, avg token latency 160ms, p95 820ms, p99 1.3s. With KV warmup on the aggressive run tokens/sec was 19k and p95 dropped to 720ms.
[05:32] Carlos: 19k tokens/sec is great but p95 still high. Is there an intermediate config?
[05:37] Priya: yes — 35ms / concurrency 96 gave 13.5k TPS with p95 ~420-480ms. That's closer to your 12k target. We can try weighted concurrency and request-priority to bring p95 under 400ms.
[05:52] Tom: what about model slicing or using distillation? Not preferred but possible.
[05:56] Jordan: those are bigger changes; for POC we should focus on runtime knobs first. Distillation is a separate project.
[06:02] Sana: anything on batching algorithm? You mentioned continuous vs windowed batching.
[06:07] Priya: continuous batching aggregates requests up to a max window or token count; windowed batching waits fixed time slices. For mixed workloads continuous with adaptive window that shrinks when queue length grows works best. We tuned an adaptive window and saw improved p95 at same throughput compared to static 50ms.
[06:27] [10:00] (mid-call details and logs review — discussion of specific trace lines and sample payloads; a few side conversations)
[10:12] Carlos: I'm going to ask the platform team to share traces; do you need full request payloads or can we redact?
[10:20] Priya: redacted payloads are fine so long as sequence length and tokenization align. Also include timestamp, route id, and whether KV cache hit.
[10:30] Carlos: ok will do.
[10:33] Priya: for the sustained run we saw occasional GC spikes on sidecar that caused brief pauses; not Redwood runtime but your edge proxy. If you can add a small connection pool tuning it reduces tail jitter.
[10:48] Tom: noted. We'll ask SRE.
[11:00] Priya: one more operational note — set route-level fallbacks for overloaded periods: degrade to smaller model or rerank-only flow. That avoids queue blowups.
[11:12] Jordan: customers we've seen switch to a two-tier routing: primary model for normal traffic, fallback small model for spikes. Does that match your appetite?
[11:20] Tom: yes we can accept a fallback for spikes under 10% of traffic but must preserve end-to-end SLOs.
[11:28] Sana: how do we measure ROI for batching changes?
[11:32] Priya: token cost curves — we can show cost per 1k tokens before vs after tuning; also show GPU utilization and required replica count at target QPS. We'll produce a short slide.
[11:45] Jordan: action items recap in a bit. Priya any other tuning to try?
[11:50] Priya: we'll run the 1-hour sustained tests with target concurrency profiles (64, 96, 128) and adaptive windowing; we'll also force kernel variants for one run to compare GA kernels.
[12:02] Carlos: for the forced kernel runs do you expect to break anything? Can they be done in staging?
[12:07] Priya: done in staging only, safe. We'll log perf counters.
[12:12] Tom: what about end-to-end user latency including network? Our SLO includes 200ms network budget.
[12:19] Priya: yes we'll include a small network emulation in one run to approximate production cross-region latency. That will give more realistic p95.
[12:30] Jordan: okay any blockers for next week?
[12:33] Carlos: only that we need to get traces out today, I'll follow up after the call.
[12:38] Jordan: perfect. Quick recap of next steps: Priya runs sustained tests and shares raw logs; Jordan sends pricing & burst options; Carlos sends traces and target QPS. We'll schedule kernel deep-dive later in Feb.
[12:52] Tom: thanks everyone.
[12:55] Jordan: thanks, end.

Notes on transcription: small speaker mislabels and some engine names mangled (e.g., a100_v2_sim, gemm_opt_v3). Stutters and filler words present.
